fixes.explanation: The writer is a king, so I see why the king came to mind (Ecclesiastes 1:1). But he never says they answer to him. He says "There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked…" Same fate, no ranking.

True. The Teacher says "…the hearts of men are full of evil and madness while they are alive…" That's a hard line, and he doesn't dress it up. The very next verse says "There is hope, however, for anyone who is among the living…" (Ecclesiastes 9:4).
He never says that here. What he says the living know is "…that they will die…" He goes on to say there is no work in Sheol (Ecclesiastes 9:10). Nothing in this stretch promises the work will last.

He doesn't give that as the reason. Verse 9 does mention "…your labor under the sun." But the reason he gives for the bread and wine is that God has already approved your works. Nothing in the verse says the labor has come to an end.

False is right. The Teacher says "…the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun…" and "…all your fleeting days." He calls it fleeting, not long and lasting. And the verse opens with the words "Enjoy life…"

All your might. The Teacher says "Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might…" That means full effort, no coasting. When I stamp a cookie, my mustache and I go in so hard the flour files a complaint.
Fish in a cruel net. The Teacher says men are ensnared "Like fish caught in a cruel net or birds trapped in a snare…" Two pictures of being caught. He says the evil time "…suddenly falls upon them."

Sheep show up in plenty of Bible pictures, but not in this one. Here the Teacher says men are like fish caught in a cruel net or birds trapped in a snare. Being caught is the picture. Good guess, but this verse sends you to the water and the sky instead.
